name: Quiet Hall
tagline: Exam nerves handled: the night before, in the room, after
about: Quiet Hall is a pocket toolkit for exam anxiety: a night-before plan, a 60-second reset for panic in the room, a strategy for when your mind goes blank, a stop to the post-exam spiral, and help requesting the support you are entitled to.
persona: You are a university counsellor trained in CBT and exam-stress support: warm, concrete, never dismissive, and clear about when a student should speak to a professional.

onboarding.title: Walk in steadier
onboarding.subtitle: A little about how anxiety shows up for you makes the tools sharper.

profile.label: Anything that's helped before
profile.placeholder: walking, breathing app, talking to a friend

tools.title: Night-before plan
tools.subtitle: Sleep, bag, brain, all sorted
tools.prompt: Exam: {exam}. Feeling: {feeling}. Bedtime: {bedtime}. Produce steps for the evening with clock times working back from bedtime (light-review cap, food, screens, wind-down, what to do if sleep doesn't come), a checklist for the bag and the morning (ID, permitted items, route, breakfast), a callout on why the all-nighter loses marks, and a quote with a short, believable sentence to say to yourself when the worry starts.

tools.title: Panic in the room
tools.subtitle: 60 seconds to get back to the paper
tools.prompt: Symptom: {symptom}. Time left: {left}. Give steps for a 60-second reset that can be done silently at a desk (breathing count, grounding on the paper, posture, one micro-task), then bullets on re-entering the exam given the time left (which question to pick first, how to bank easy marks), a quote with a three-word cue to write in the margin, and a callout on when and how to signal an invigilator and what they can do.

tools.title: Mind went blank
tools.subtitle: Retrieve it, or earn partial credit
tools.prompt: Blank on: {topic}. Question type: {qtype}. Provide steps for cued retrieval (rewrite the question in your own words, list any related word, sketch a diagram, recall the lecture's context) taking under 3 minutes, bullets of partial-credit tactics specific to this question type (define terms, state the method, show structure), a table (If you remember only… | Write this) with 4 rows, and a quote with a starting sentence that opens the answer without committing to facts you don't have yet.

tools.title: Post-exam spiral
tools.subtitle: Stop replaying it

inputs.label: What you keep replaying
inputs.placeholder: I think I misread question 3 and everyone said it was easy

tools.prompt: Replaying: {replay}. Next: {next}. Write a table (Thought | Evidence for | Evidence against | More balanced thought) for the 2 strongest worries, text on why post-mortems with classmates inflate anxiety and rarely change marks, steps for the next 3 hours that close the loop (one-line note of anything to check later, movement, food, a firm rule on not discussing answers), and a callout on signs the spiral is more than exam stress and who to contact at a university (counselling, GP, crisis line).

tools.title: Ask for adjustments
tools.subtitle: Extra time, separate room, deferrals

inputs.label: Your situation
inputs.placeholder: diagnosed anxiety, panic attacks in exam halls, no formal support yet

tools.prompt: Situation: {situation}. Looking for: {want}. Give bullets of the adjustments universities commonly offer for anxiety and the evidence usually required (without promising what any institution will grant), a checklist of steps from first contact to the exam with typical lead times, a quote with an email to the disability or wellbeing service requesting a meeting that states the need without over-disclosing, and a callout on deadlines: adjustments are often needed weeks before the exam period.

disclaimer: Quiet Hall offers general coping strategies, not therapy or diagnosis. If anxiety is affecting daily life, or you have thoughts of harming yourself, contact your university wellbeing service, a doctor or a crisis line now.
